summary: This work demonstrates interface piezoelectricity as a dissipation mechanism in superconducting qubits fabricated on high-resistivity silicon by integrating a transmon qubit into a surface acoustic wave resonator, observing up to 50% reduction in qubit lifetime $T_1$ when tuned into resonance with mechanical modes. Finite-element simulations predict that interface piezoelectric loss scales as $\Gamma_{\mathrm{piezo}} \propto f_q^{3.4}$ and will dominate over two-level system loss above approximately 10 GHz, posing a critical challenge for millimeter-wave superconducting qubits.
motivation: While two-level systems have been identified as a primary loss channel in superconducting qubits on nominally non-piezoelectric substrates like silicon, recent classical measurements revealed an effective piezoelectric response at metal-dielectric interfaces despite bulk centrosymmetry; whether this coupling limits qubit coherence has remained unknown.
method: A floating transmon SQUID shunted by an interdigital transducer (IDT) serving simultaneously as the qubit capacitor and electromechanical transducer was embedded in a Bragg-reflector-defined SAW resonator on 50 nm aluminum on high-resistivity silicon. Qubit lifetime $T_1$ and coherence $T_2^*$ were measured as functions of qubit frequency; piezoelectric signatures were isolated by applying a DC bias voltage $V_{\mathrm{bias}}$ to distinguish field-insensitive mechanical resonances from Stark-tunable two-level system defects.
result: Extracted electromechanical coupling strengths $g_{m,k}/2\pi \sim 100$ kHz and SAW mode linewidths $\kappa_{m,k}/2\pi \sim 1$ MHz across three samples; simulations yielded $\tan\delta_{\mathrm{piezo}} \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-4}$ at 4.5 GHz (subdominant to state-of-the-art TLS loss of $10^{-3}$) but predict crossover frequency near 10 GHz where interface piezoelectric loss becomes comparable to and subsequently exceeds TLS-limited dissipation.
